La métaphore remonte au moins à Cicéron: The metaphor goes back at least to Cicero: in the Laelius, he describes the Republic that "glides readily down the path of ruin when once it has taken a start". In 1910, Alfred Sidgwick described it as an argument, the "thin end of a wedge" objection.
Dans la Grèce antique, la nature servait: In Ancient Greece, nature already served as a model for how to act. Rousseau replied: "We do not know what our nature permits us to be."
L'expression américaine « sauter dans le: The American phrase "jump on the bandwagon" comes from the 1848 presidential campaign: circus clown Dan Rice invited candidate Zachary Taylor onto his circus bandwagon. In 1951, Solomon Asch measured this conformity in the lab.
Le nom latin, argumentum ad ignorantiam,: The Latin name, argumentum ad ignorantiam, was probably coined by John Locke in the late 17th century. Carl Sagan used to point out: "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence."
Tu quoque veut dire « toi aussi » en lat: Tu quoque means "you also" in Latin. In the 1930s Soviet Union, American criticism was met with: "And you are lynching Negroes."
Le latin dit « après ceci, donc à cause: The Latin says "after this, therefore because of this". The footballer Pelé blamed a slump on a shirt he had given away; it ended when a friend brought one back… which was not the original.
Aristote décrit cette « pétition de prin: Aristotle described this "begging the question" in the Prior Analytics and the Topics: asking to be granted the very point at issue. The Latin term petitio principii passed into English in the 16th century.
C'est John Locke qui a forgé l'expressio: John Locke coined the phrase argumentum ad verecundiam, the appeal to modesty: people dare not contradict authority. In 1923, Theophilus Painter counted 24 pairs of human chromosomes; researchers repeated the figure out of deference for decades, though there are 23.
L'anthropologue Eugenie Scott invente le: The anthropologist Eugenie Scott coined the term in 1994, after the creationist Duane Gish, whom she considered the technique's most avid practitioner.
La dispute scolastique suivait des règle: Scholastic disputation followed fixed rules and relied on written authorities. There were also famous public disputations, such as Barcelona in 1263, where Nachmanides defended Judaism, or Leipzig in 1519 between Luther and Eck.
L'« homme d'acier » est l'inverse de l'h: The steel man is the opposite of the straw man, a term whose sense of an easily knocked-down opponent is recorded around 1620. The straw man fallacy only entered a logic textbook in 1956.
Le programmeur italien Alberto Brandolin: The Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini stated it in January 2013, after reading Kahneman and then watching a Berlusconi–Travaglio debate. Jonathan Swift had already written in 1710: "Falsehood flies, and truth comes limping after it."
Anatol Rapoport, mathématicien et spécia: Anatol Rapoport, a mathematician and game theorist, won Robert Axelrod's computer tournament in the 1980s with "tit for tat", a four-line program that starts by cooperating.
Karl Popper en fait le critère de la sci: Karl Popper made it the criterion of science in 1934: you would have to see every swan to prove they are white, but a single black swan is enough to refute it. In maths, Euler's sum of powers conjecture fell in 1966 to a single counterexample.
La controverse se tient au collège San G: The debate was held at the Colegio de San Gregorio in Valladolid, before a panel of doctors and theologians assembled by Charles V, who halted further conquest meanwhile. Both sides claimed victory, but the panel never reached a joint decision.
Lors du premier débat, le 26 septembre 1: At the first debate, on 26 September 1960 in Chicago, Nixon refused make-up and his stubble showed on screen. He had just come out of hospital after a knee infection.
Dans les premiers dialogues de Platon, S: In Plato's early dialogues, Socrates made it a method: he led his interlocutor step by step to an absurd conclusion, forcing him to give up his claim. Euclid proved this way that there are infinitely many primes.
Brendan Nyhan est l'un des chercheurs qu: Brendan Nyhan was one of the researchers who proposed this effect. A 2020 review noted widespread failures to replicate it, and Nyhan himself wrote in 2021 that the persistence of misinformation is mostly due to other factors.
La Poétique, vers 335 av. J.-C., est le: The Poetics, around 335 BC, is the oldest surviving work of Greek dramatic theory. Its second part, on comedy, is lost; Umberto Eco made it the core of The Name of the Rose.
Joseph Campbell publie Le Héros aux mill: Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces in 1949 and borrowed the word "monomyth" from James Joyce's Finnegans Wake. George Lucas acknowledged its influence on Star Wars.
Propp publie Morphologie du conte en rus: Propp published Morphology of the Folktale in Russian in 1928, based on 100 tales from Alexander Afanasyev's collection. The book went unnoticed in the West until its 1958 English translation, then influenced Lévi-Strauss and Barthes.
L'expression vient d'Horace, dans son Ar: The phrase comes from Horace, in his Ars Poetica, around 13 BC: the good epic poet "hurries to the action and snatches the listener into the middle of things", like Homer, whose Iliad begins in the ninth year of the Trojan War.
Tchekhov l'écrit dans une lettre de 1889: Chekhov wrote it in an 1889 letter: "One must not put a loaded rifle on the stage if no one is thinking of firing it." An irony noted by Donald Rayfield: in one of his own plays, two loaded firearms are never fired.
L'expression est forgée par le critique: The phrase was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in 1961, in The Rhetoric of Fiction. Huckleberry Finn, Holden Caulfield and Humbert Humbert are classic examples.
Les plus anciennes mentions en font la t: The earliest mentions describe it as an Arabic translation of a lost Persian book, Hezār Afsān, "A Thousand Tales". Antoine Galland translated it into French from 1704 to 1717 and added Aladdin and Ali Baba, told to him by the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab.
Le mot ironie vient du grec eirōneía, au: The word irony comes from the Greek eirōneía, in the 5th century BC, and from the comedy character who pretends to know less than he does. Dramatic irony gives the audience what the characters do not know.
La phrase « Ne me dis pas que la lune br: The line "Don't tell me the moon is shining; show me the glint of light on broken glass" is attributed to Chekhov, but it is a summary. In an 1886 letter to his brother, he advised seizing on small details, such as a shard of bottle glass glinting on a mill dam.
Dans le théâtre grec, une grue faisait d: In Greek theatre, a crane lowered the actor playing the god. More than half of Euripides' surviving tragedies end this way. Aristotle wanted the resolution to arise from the plot itself, and Horace kept it for a knot "worthy of a god".
Le 28 août 1963, devant plus de 250 000: On 28 August 1963, before over 250,000 people at the Lincoln Memorial, King left his text: the singer Mahalia Jackson shouted "Tell 'em about the dream, Martin!". The "I have a dream" passage was improvised.
Churchill prononce cette phrase le 13 ma: Churchill spoke this line on 13 May 1940 in the Commons, in his first speech as Prime Minister. Garibaldi had offered his men in 1849 "hunger, thirst, forced marches, battle, and death", and Theodore Roosevelt spoke in 1897 of "blood and sweat and tears".
Le 19 novembre 1863, l'orateur vedette E: On 19 November 1863, the star speaker Edward Everett spoke for about two hours; Lincoln, for two minutes. The next day Everett wrote to him that he wished he had come as near the central idea in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
L'appel est lancé à 22 h, heure de Londr: The appeal went out at 10 pm London time. The BBC did not keep the recording, and few French listeners heard it; the British government had almost withdrawn permission. The speech of 22 June was far more widely heard.
Badinter avait sauvé Patrick Henry de la: Badinter had saved Patrick Henry from the guillotine in January 1977; the last execution in France took place on 10 September 1977. After his speech, the Assembly voted for abolition on 18 September 1981 by 363 votes to 117, and the law was promulgated on 9 October.
Le débat est d'une hostilité exceptionne: The debate was exceptionally hostile, with personal attacks on Simone Veil and her family. The law was adopted on 17 January 1975. In July 2018, Simone Veil was interred in the Panthéon.
Kennedy parle le 26 juin 1963 devant la: Kennedy spoke on 26 June 1963 outside Rathaus Schöneberg, in West Berlin, before about 120,000 people. In his notes, he had written the line phonetically: "ish bin ein Bearleener".
La légende du beignet semble venir du ro: The doughnut legend seems to come from Len Deighton's 1983 spy novel Berlin Game, then a 1988 New York Times op-ed. Kennedy's sentence is correct, and the crowd laughed later, at a joke about his interpreter.
Thucydide la rapporte au livre II de son: Thucydides reports it in Book II of his History of the Peloponnesian War, at the end of the first year of the war. He warns that his speeches are not verbatim, and Plato, in the Menexenus, attributes it to Aspasia, Pericles' companion.
La Première Philippique date de 351-350: The First Philippic dates from 351-350 BC. According to Plutarch, Demosthenes had overcome his stammer by speaking with pebbles in his mouth. Cicero would reuse the title Philippics for his speeches against Mark Antony.
La lettre paraît le 13 janvier 1898 en u: The letter appeared on 13 January 1898 on the front page of L'Aurore, Georges Clemenceau's daily, addressed to President Félix Faure. Zola was convicted of libel on 23 February 1898 and went into exile in England until June 1899.
Le 9 octobre 2012, à 15 ans, Malala Yous: On 9 October 2012, aged 15, Malala Yousafzai had been shot by a Taliban gunman on a bus in the Swat valley. The UN named 12 July 2013 "Malala Day". In 2014, aged 17, she became the youngest Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
Le mot vient de la Congregatio de Propag: The word comes from the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, created in 1622 by the Catholic Church to "propagate the faith" during the Counter-Reformation. It stayed neutral until the First World War, when it became pejorative.
Neveu de Sigmund Freud, Edward Bernays s: A nephew of Sigmund Freud, Edward Bernays used his uncle's ideas. In 1929 he had women smoke in public under the slogan "torches of freedom", and he later worked for United Fruit at the time of the 1954 coup in Guatemala.
L'effet est identifié en 1977 par Lynn H: The effect was identified in 1977 by Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino, at Villanova and Temple universities. In 2015, a study showed that knowing the right answer does not protect against a repeated falsehood.
Hitler emploie l'expression « große Lüge: Hitler used the phrase "große Lüge" in Mein Kampf, in 1925, to accuse the Jews. A US intelligence (OSS) report on Hitler, around 1943, summed up the idea. The line often attributed to Goebbels has no source.
1984 paraît en 1949. Orwell explique la: Nineteen Eighty-Four came out in 1949. Orwell explained Newspeak in an appendix, "The Principles of Newspeak". It resembles the Basic English proposed in 1930 by the linguist Charles Kay Ogden.
Le rapport de 2016 est signé Christopher: The 2016 report was written by Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews. It identifies four features: many channels, rapid and continuous repetition, no commitment to objective reality, no commitment to consistency. Russia applied it notably to the annexation of Crimea.
Le psychologue William McGuire développe: The psychologist William McGuire developed this "inoculation" theory in 1961, on the model of a vaccine. Games such as Bad News or Harmony Square and short videos apply it.
Le terme est attribué au sénateur texan: The term is credited to Texas senator Lloyd Bentsen in 1985: flooded with letters paid for by insurers, he said a fellow from Texas can tell the difference between grass roots and AstroTurf, a brand of artificial grass.
En 1988, Richard Morin, du Washington Po: In 1988, Richard Morin of the Washington Post spoke of a "Dog Whistle Effect" about polls where one word changes everything. The term entered Australian politics in the mid-1990s, then Britain in 2005 with the adviser Lynton Crosby.
Diffusée le 30 octobre 1938 sur CBS, vei: Broadcast on 30 October 1938 on CBS, on Halloween eve, the show was heard by only 2% of households according to a Hooper survey. Newspapers inflated the rare cases of fear, and Hadley Cantril's 1940 study is considered seriously flawed.
Joseph Overton, du Mackinac Center for P: Joseph Overton, of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, described in the early 1990s a spectrum of more or less acceptable ideas. After his death, his colleague Joseph Lehman developed the concept and named it after him.
En 1981, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1981, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman offered a choice of treatment for 600 patients: framed as "saves 200 lives", it was chosen by 72% of participants. Changing only the presentation changes the choice.
